strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in statistical theory (probability integral transform); elegant connection between distributional calibration and avoiding noise overfitting
Rigorous theoretical analysis including convergence behavior (Section 4) and formal proofs in appendices; clear exposition of early-stage and late-stage optimization dynamics
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple applications (DIP denoising, PET reconstruction, 1D deconvolution) with extensive reproducibility details and multiple noise models
Solid practical implementation details including tail approximations (Appendix C) and numerical stability solutions for Gaussian/Poisson/clipped-Gaussian noise
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations (Section 6.2) acknowledging scope restrictions and cases where DC loss may not apply
Consistent empirical improvements demonstrated across applications: DIP-DC removes need for early stopping and achieves higher peak PSNR; PET-DC shows better noise-detail trade-offs
weaknesses: Critical theoretical gap: Small DC loss does not guarantee small signal error (Appendix B.3); worst-case scenario shows 2× worse error than MSE possible (Eq. 7); this fundamental non-equivalence undermines core theoretical narrative and is insufficiently emphasized in main text

Severe computational overhead inadequately addressed: 600× slower than MSE at N=1,000,000 (Table 2, 0.5s vs 0.0008s); dismissed as 'not a bottleneck' but prohibitive for practical large-scale deployment; O(N log N) sorting cost could be substantial

Substantial scope limitations significantly reduce impact: requires known noise model (major limitation for medical imaging with model mismatch); needs many independent measurements; fails for correlated/poorly-characterized noise; these represent entire application domains

Modest empirical improvements with incomplete baselines: DIP results show ~1-2 dB improvements with overlapping error bars (Figure 5d); PET results only on synthetic BrainWeb phantoms, no real clinical validation; missing comparisons with robust loss functions (Huber, smooth L1) and recent denoising methods

Discrete noise handling imperfect: naive PIT for Poisson produces non-uniform CDFs (acknowledged in Appendix A.3); authors mention randomized PIT alternative but don't implement; Figure F1 shows substantial deviation from uniformity, undermining theoretical foundation for count data

Regularization interaction insufficiently explored: DC loss defines equivalence class of solutions (Figure 2), not unique solution; final quality depends critically on regularizer and optimization path; benefit diminishes if careful regularization tuning still required; sensitivity to hyperparameter β not thoroughly analyzed

Missing related work and comparisons: limited engagement with robust loss functions, calibration methods in ML, and likelihood-based overfitting-prevention approaches; baseline comparisons limited to conventional MSE/NLL rather than state-of-the-art alternatives

Limited experimental scope: PET experiments only synthetic data; only 5 random seeds for DIP with overlapping error bars; missing ablations on metric choice (Wasserstein vs alternatives), sensitivity to noise model mismatch, and comparison with other regularization approaches

strengths: Mathematically rigorous formulation grounded in probability integral transform with clear geometric intuition (Figure 1)
Comprehensive mathematical treatment including tail approximations and theoretical analysis in appendices
Demonstrates practical benefits across multiple application domains (DIP denoising, PET reconstruction, 1D deconvolution)
Handles multiple noise models (Gaussian, Poisson, clipped Gaussian) with appropriate implementations
Honest discussion of limitations and theoretical gaps (DC loss defining equivalence classes, non-guarantees of superior solutions)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily applies well-established statistical concepts (PIT from 1938, goodness-of-fit testing) to inverse problems; lacks significant technical innovation
Critical theoretical gap: Appendix B.3 proves small DC loss does NOT imply small error; worst-case DC error can be 2× worse than MSE, undermining core motivation
Substantial computational overhead: 230× slower than NLL at N=1M samples; 24× slower backward pass; dismissed without adequate justification
Narrow experimental evaluation: only DIP and PET demonstrations; missing comparisons to modern calibration methods, Bayesian approaches, and other overfitting solutions for neural inverse problems
Discrete noise implementation compromise: acknowledges Poisson CDF non-uniformity is fundamental but uses naive PIT for simplicity, contradicting theoretical claims

Regularization mechanism unexplained: Section 4.2 claim that manifold of solutions is preferable to unique optimum is intuitive hand-waving, not rigorous analysis; optimal β differs significantly between methods (Figure 8a)

Overclaimed practical significance: modest peak PSNR improvements in DIP (~0.5-1 dB); early stopping removal is minor benefit since early stopping is fast and standard; PET benefits limited to specific TV+regularized setting
Insufficient scope analysis: requires known noise model, many independent measurements, single realization per measurement; applicability to misspecified noise and ill-posed problems unclear
Statistical rigor issues: inconsistent error bars across experiments; modest differences relative to uncertainty; limited statistical testing to validate claimed improvements
Misleading claims: abstract states method avoids overfitting 'without use of priors' but all experiments use implicit/explicit regularization (DIP network architecture, PET TV penalty)

strengths: Novel distributional consistency perspective on data-fidelity terms with clear theoretical motivation grounded in probability integral transform
Comprehensive theoretical analysis including both early-stage optimization behavior (Section 4.1) and characterization of solution manifolds (Appendix B)
Extensive and well-designed experiments across multiple domains (image denoising, PET reconstruction, 1D deconvolution) with varied noise models and thorough ablations
Excellent practical implementation with detailed numerical handling for stability (tail approximations, Poisson-Gamma duality) and concrete algorithms for reproducibility
Strong empirical results demonstrating consistent benefits: eliminates early stopping requirement for DIP, improves noise-detail tradeoffs with TV regularization in PET
Clear and honest discussion of limitations with well-organized supplementary material providing extensive implementation details and additional experiments
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation: low DC loss does not guarantee low signal error (Appendix B.3), with worst-case example showing 2× higher error than MSE despite lower DC loss, making regularization essential rather than optional

Significantly restricted applicability: requires known noise model, many independent measurements, single measurement per index—excludes small-data regimes, misspecified noise, and correlated measurements
Substantial computational overhead: 20-30× slower than MSE/NLL at N=1,000 and 0.5s vs. 0.001s for N=1,000,000 (Appendix G), limiting large-scale deployment despite claimed practicality

Incomplete theoretical treatment of discrete noise: Poisson experiments use naive PIT while proposed randomized alternative remains unimplemented; CDF histograms show pathological behavior at low doses (Figure F1)
Limited baseline comparisons: no evaluation against other calibration-based or noise-robust losses, and connection to method-noise literature (Buades et al. 2005) mentioned but not explored

Marginal practical improvements in some scenarios: 1-3 dB PSNR gains for DIP, diminishing returns when regularization must be carefully tuned anyway; no large-scale experiments or integration with learned priors
